propositions.text: Applicant Pritam Singh Shah seeks judicial review of Immigration Officer's refusal of his Permanent Residence application on H&C grounds.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, Pritam Singh Shah, seeks judicial review of the decision of an Immigration Officer [the Officer], dated November 15, 2018, which refused his Application for Permanent Residence from within Canada on Humanitarian and Compassionate [H&C] grounds, pursuant to section 25(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27 [the Act].

paragraphs.summary: Applicant Shah seeks judicial review of an Immigration Officer's refusal of his Permanent Residence application on H&C grounds.

propositions.text: The Application is dismissed as the Officer's decision is reasonable, justified, transparent, intelligible, and defensible.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, the Application is dismissed. While the Court sympathizes with the Applicant’s circumstances and his desire to remain in Canada with his family, the Court’s role is not to make the decision, rather to determine if the Officer’s decision is reasonable. The Court finds that the decision is reasonable; it is justified, transparent and intelligible and is defensible in accordance with the law and the facts on the record.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses the Application, finding the Officer's decision reasonable and defensible despite sympathy for Applicant.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah is a 78-year-old Indian citizen with family in Canada who helped raise his grandchildren and impart culture.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah is a 78-year-old citizen of India. His only family ‒ his son, daughter-in-law and two grandsons ‒ arrived in Canada in 2010 and are now permanent residents. Prior to 2010 Mr. Shah lived with his family in India. He attests that his family is very close and that he helped raise his grandchildren, imparting his traditional culture and language.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant Shah is a 78-year-old Indian citizen with family in Canada and close family ties.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah's daughter-in-law and youngest grandson returned to India to care for him; caretaker neglected him causing isolation and poor health.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah recounts that his daughter-in-law and youngest grandson returned to India shortly after their arrival in Canada in 2010 to care for him. Before returning to Canada in 2012, Mr. Shah’s daughter-in-law arranged for a caretaker for Mr. Shah. He attests that the caretaker neglected him, leaving him in isolation and poor mental and physical health.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant states daughter-in-law and grandson returned to India to care for him but caretaker neglected him causing poor health.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah obtained a multiple entry Temporary Residence Visa in 2015 valid until 2025 allowing stays up to six months.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah has visited Canada several times. On March 26, 2015, he obtained a multiple entry Temporary Residence Visa [TRV], which expires on January 13, 2025. This multiple entry TRV permits Mr. Shah to remain in Canada for periods of up to six months with possible extensions.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant obtained a multiple entry TRV in 2015 valid until 2025 allowing six-month stays.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah applied for Permanent Residence on H&C grounds in June 2017 citing establishment, family ties, separation impact, frail health, and best interests of grandsons.
propositions.quote: In April 2017, Mr. Shah entered Canada as a visitor. On June 15, 2017, Mr. Shah applied for Permanent Residence from within Canada on H&C grounds, noting in particular: his establishment in Canada, family ties, the impact of separation from his family, his frail health and the best interest of his grandsons.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant applied for Permanent Residence on H&C grounds citing family ties, health, and best interests of grandsons.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah arrived in Canada again in February 2018 and has remained due to TRV extension.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah arrived in Canada again in February 2018 and has remained since due to the extension of his TRV.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant arrived in Canada in February 2018 and stayed due to TRV extension.

propositions.text: Applicant's family submitted online interests to sponsor him but were unsuccessful due to program closure and high volume.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah’s family in Canada also submitted online “an interest to sponsor a family member or grandparent” in 2017 but their application was not selected. In January 2019, Mr. Shah’s son attempted to file another online interest, but the program closed due to high volume before he could do so.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant's family tried to sponsor him online but applications were not selected or program closed.

propositions.text: Officer considered evidence and factors, found several positive factors but denied H&C exemption on global assessment.
propositions.quote: The Officer considered the relevant evidence and factors. The Officer noted that there were several positive factors but, based on his global assessment, found that an H&C exemption was not justified.

paragraphs.summary: Officer considered evidence and denied H&C exemption based on global assessment.

propositions.text: Officer gave positive weight to Mr. Shah's compliance with immigration regulations and visits to Canada.
propositions.quote: With respect to Mr. Shah’s establishment in Canada, the Officer noted that Mr. Shah had visited Canada several times and gave positive weight to the fact that Mr. Shah had always complied with Canadian immigration regulations and had returned to India when required.

paragraphs.summary: Officer positively weighed Applicant's compliance with immigration rules and visits to Canada.

propositions.text: Officer noted Mr. Shah's investments and pension enabling independent living in India and son's support if needed.
propositions.quote: The Officer noted that Mr. Shah had some investments and a monthly pension that would enable him to live independently in India. The Officer also noted that Mr. Shah’s son would support him if needed whether he returned to India or remained in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Officer noted Applicant's financial means and son's support in India or Canada.

propositions.text: Officer gave little weight to Mr. Shah's time in Canada since February 2018 as establishment factor.
propositions.quote: The Officer noted that Mr. Shah has resided with his family in Canada continuously since February 2018, but gave little weight to his time spent in Canada as a factor supporting his establishment.

paragraphs.summary: Officer gave little weight to Applicant's recent continuous residence in Canada as establishment.

propositions.text: Officer gave significant positive weight to Mr. Shah's family relationship and acknowledged no relatives in India.
propositions.quote: The Officer gave significant positive weight to Mr. Shah’s relationship with his family. The Officer acknowledged that Mr. Shah had no relatives in India and that his only family is his son, daughter-in-law and grandsons in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Officer gave significant weight to Applicant's family ties and lack of relatives in India.

propositions.text: Officer gave little weight to family separation impact due to lack of corroborative evidence and Mr. Shah's fitness to travel.
propositions.quote: The Officer gave little weight to the impact of family separation. The Officer found that there was little corroborative evidence to explain why Mr. Shah was not capable of living on his own and required day-to-day support or assistance. The Officer noted that Mr. Shah had recently passed the medical examination to permit his TRV to be extended. The Officer added that Mr. Shah’s multiple entry visa, valid until 2025, would permit him to continue to visit his family in Canada and noted that there was little evidence to suggest that he is not fit to travel or would experience difficulty doing so. The Officer also noted that there was little evidence that he would not be able to return to India based on his age.

paragraphs.summary: Officer gave little weight to family separation impact due to lack of evidence and Applicant's fitness to travel.

propositions.text: Officer noted oldest grandson is 19 and does not meet 'child' definition for BIOC analysis.
propositions.quote: With respect to the best interests of the children affected [BIOC] ‒ i.e., Mr. Shah’s grandsons ‒ the Officer noted that the oldest grandson was 19 years of age and did not meet the definition of “child” for the purposes of the BIOC analysis.

paragraphs.summary: Officer noted oldest grandson is 19 and excluded from BIOC analysis.

propositions.text: Officer found little evidence of Mr. Shah's role in younger grandson's life; grandson's needs met without him.
propositions.quote: With respect to Mr. Shah’s 17-year-old grandson, the Officer found that there was little evidence of Mr. Shah’s role in his younger grandson’s life. The Officer concluded that the grandson’s basic medical, educational, and social needs would continue to be met in Mr. Shah’s absence.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found little evidence of Applicant's role in younger grandson's life; needs met without him.

propositions.text: Officer concluded H&C factors globally did not justify exemption under subsection 25(1) of the Act.
propositions.quote: In conclusion, the Officer found that the H&C factors, assessed globally, did not warrant an exemption under subsection 25(1) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: Officer concluded H&C factors did not justify exemption under the Act.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah argues decision is unreasonable due to failure to consider his circumstances and errors in assessing best interests of younger grandson.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah submits that the decision is not reasonable: the Officer erred by failing to consider the evidence of his circumstances as a whole in relation to the hardships he would face if required to return to India; and, the Officer erred in his assessment of the best interests of his younger grandson, by ignoring relevant evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues decision is unreasonable due to failure to consider circumstances and errors in best interests assessment.

propositions.text: Standard of review for Officer's H&C decision is reasonableness per Kanthasamy at para 44.
propositions.quote: The jurisprudence has clearly established that the standard of review of an Officer’s decision with respect to an H&C application is reasonableness (Kanthasamy v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61, [2015] 3 SCR 909 [Kanthasamy] at para 44).

paragraphs.summary: Standard of review for Officer's H&C decision is reasonableness per Kanthasamy.

propositions.text: Reasonableness requires justification, transparency, intelligibility, and defensible outcomes per Dunsmuir at para 47.
propositions.quote: To determine whether a decision is reasonable, the Court looks for “the existence of justification, transparency and intelligibility within the decision-making process” and considers “whether the decision falls within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes which are defensible in respect of the facts and law” (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at para 47, [2008] 1 SCR 190).

paragraphs.summary: Reasonableness requires justification, transparency, intelligibility, and defensible outcomes per Dunsmuir.

propositions.text: The Court must defer to the decision-maker and intervene only if the decision fails the Dunsmuir standard.
propositions.quote: The Court owes deference to the decision-maker and should only intervene where the decision does not reflect the Dunsmuir standard.

propositions.text: The Court's role is not to remake the decision or reweigh evidence.
propositions.quote: The role of the Court is not to remake the decision or to reweigh the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states it must defer to the decision-maker and not remake the decision or reweigh evidence, intervening only if the Dunsmuir standard is not met.

propositions.text: The H&C Officer failed to consider relevant evidence of hardship from unique circumstances including family dependency, lack of social network, and advanced age.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah submits that the H&C Officer failed to consider relevant evidence of the hardship he would face resulting from his unique circumstances, including his emotional and physical dependency on his family in Canada, his lack of a social network in India, and his inability to create new networks due to his advanced age.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah argues the Officer failed to consider hardship evidence related to his family dependency, social network absence, and age.

propositions.text: Age and family dependency are important factors in assessing hardship, supported by cited cases Makarenko and Epstein.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah submits that his age and family dependency are important factors that should be considered in assessing hardship (Makarenko v Canada...; Epstein v Canada...).

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah argues age and family dependency are key hardship factors, citing Makarenko and Epstein.

propositions.text: The Officer failed to consider evidence holistically, instead considering factors in segments causing contradictory findings, contrary to Kanthasamy.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah further submits that the Officer did not consider the evidence holistically, contrary to the principle in Kanthasamy at para 113.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah argues the Officer did not consider evidence holistically, leading to contradictory findings, against Kanthasamy.

propositions.text: The Officer did not follow Supreme Court guidance in Baker requiring substantial weight to children's best interests.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah submits that the Officer did not follow the guidance of the Supreme Court of Canada in Baker... requiring decision-makers to “consider children’s best interests as an important factor, give them substantial weight...

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah argues the Officer failed to follow Baker's guidance on giving substantial weight to children's best interests.

propositions.text: The Officer ignored evidence of Mr. Shah's relationship with his younger grandson, including photos and a letter from the older grandson.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah submits that the Officer ignored relevant evidence of his relationship with his younger grandson... failed to consider the photographs... and the letter...

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah argues the Officer ignored evidence of his relationship with his younger grandson, including photos and a letter.

propositions.text: The Officer focused on irrelevant BIOC factors like grandson's access to Canadian services, ignoring other relevant factors.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah also submits that the Officer failed to take into account other relevant BIOC factors, focussing instead on irrelevant factors, including his grandson’s access to the Canadian medical system, education system and social services.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah argues the Officer focused on irrelevant BIOC factors, ignoring other relevant ones.

propositions.text: H&C considerations are no longer assessed via underserved and disproportionate hardships; Officer applied Kanthasamy principles and assessed all factors globally.
propositions.quote: The Respondent notes that H&C considerations are no longer assessed through the lens of underserved and disproportionate hardships... the Officer applied the principles of Kanthasamy and assessed all the relevant H&C factors.

propositions.text: No single factor prevailed; each was considered, weighted, and assessed globally.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that no single factor prevailed over any other in the Officer’s reasons, that each factor was considered, attributed weight, and that all factors were then assessed globally.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues the Officer applied Kanthasamy, assessed all H&C factors globally, and no single factor prevailed.

propositions.text: Officer noted positive factors like family ties but found little evidence for other claims like inability to live alone or travel.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the Officer noted several positive factors, including Mr. Shah’s strong family ties, but found a lack of evidence to support Mr. Shah’s other submissions...

propositions.text: Officer noted Mr. Shah's multiple entry visa permits travel to Canada, influencing weight on family separation impact.
propositions.quote: The Respondent notes that the Officer observed that the multiple entry visa, valid until 2025, permits Mr. Shah to travel to Canada... informed the Officer’s attribution of little weight to the impact of family separation.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent says the Officer noted family ties but little evidence for other claims and considered Mr. Shah's visa allowing travel.

propositions.text: Officer correctly stated law on BIOC, found older grandson not a child, reasonably assessed younger grandson's best interests.
propositions.quote: With respect to the BIOC, the Respondent submits that the Officer correctly stated the law... and reasonably assessed the BIOC of the younger grandson.

propositions.text: Officer reasonably concluded insufficient evidence that grandson's best interests would not be met if Mr. Shah returned to India.
propositions.quote: The Officer reasonably concluded that there was insufficient evidence that the grandson’s best interests would not be met if Mr. Shah returned to India.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues the Officer correctly applied BIOC law and reasonably concluded insufficient evidence against grandson's best interests.

propositions.text: Officer's decision is reasonable, addressing all relevant factors and evidence, with no error in global assessment or evidence consideration.
propositions.quote: The Officer addressed all of the factors relevant to the H&C application and all of the evidence submitted... The Officer did not err by failing to consider relevant evidence or by failing to conduct a global assessment of all the relevant evidence.

propositions.text: A reasonable decision is transparent, intelligible, and justified.
propositions.quote: a decision is reasonable where it is transparent, intelligible and justified.

propositions.text: Weight attached to considerations is within Officer's discretion; Court does not reweigh evidence.
propositions.quote: The weight attached to the considerations is within the Officer’s discretion and the Court’s role is not to reweigh the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the Officer's decision reasonable, properly considering all evidence and factors, and defers to the Officer's discretion on weight.

propositions.text: Section 25 of the Act allows discretionary exemption based on H&C considerations including best interests of a directly affected child.
propositions.quote: Section 25 of the Act... may be granted on the basis of humanitarian and compassionate considerations, “taking into account the best interests of a child directly affected”.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states section 25 allows discretionary H&C exemptions considering best interests of affected children.

propositions.text: H&C exemption is discretionary, exceptional relief, not an alternative immigration stream; onus is on applicant to prove entitlement with evidence.
propositions.quote: This exemption is discretionary and exceptional relief... The onus is at all times on an applicant to establish with sufficient evidence that this exemption or exception should be granted... Officers must consider all evidence and be satisfied relief is justified.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains H&C relief is discretionary, exceptional, not alternative immigration, and requires sufficient evidence from applicant.

propositions.text: Kanthasamy explains relief under section 25 varies with facts and context of each case.
propositions.quote: In Kanthasamy, the Supreme Court explained that what will warrant relief under section 25 will vary depending on the facts and context of each case (at para 25).

paragraphs.summary: Kanthasamy states section 25 relief depends on facts and context of each case.

propositions.text: Kanthasamy calls for liberal interpretation of H&C, weighing all relevant facts, not limited to undue hardship; some hardship is inevitable and insufficient alone.
propositions.quote: The Supreme Court also emphasized... the need to consider and weigh all relevant facts and factors and called for a more liberal interpretation of H&C considerations... some hardship is inevitable:... This alone will not generally be sufficient to warrant relief...

paragraphs.summary: Kanthasamy requires liberal H&C interpretation weighing all facts; some hardship is inevitable and insufficient alone for relief.

propositions.text: Officer considered and weighed all relevant H&C factors, including family dependency and ties, giving significant positive weight.
propositions.quote: The decision conveys that the Officer considered and weighed all the relevant H&C factors... gave “significant positive weight” to his family ties...

propositions.text: Officer reasonably found little evidence explaining inability to live alone or need for support; evidence was scant and similar.
propositions.quote: The Officer also acknowledged Mr. Shah’s submissions but reasonably concluded that there was little evidence to explain why he is unable to live on his own or why he requires support... The supporting evidence is scant...

propositions.text: No evidence Mr. Shah was in frail health or had physical/mental conditions; he passed medical exam for TRV extension.
propositions.quote: there was no evidence of that Mr. Shah was in frail health, as claimed, or suffered from any physical or mental health condition... Mr. Shah had recently passed a medical examination for the purpose of extending his TRV.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the Officer considered all H&C factors, found scant evidence of support needs or frail health, and noted medical exam passed.

propositions.text: Officer did not consider H&C factors in isolation or segments, nor make contradictory findings; conducted global assessment.
propositions.quote: Contrary to Mr. Shah’s submissions, the Officer did not consider the relevant H&C factors in isolation or in segments and did not make contradictory findings... conducted a global assessment.

propositions.text: Findings on strong family ties and ability to re-establish in India are supported and not inconsistent; they address different factors.
propositions.quote: The Officer did not make contradictory findings in noting that the family ties in Canada were strong... yet also finding that Mr. Shah would be returning to his home country... Both findings are supported by the evidence and are not inconsistent.

propositions.text: Officer made no assumption of social network in India; finding was limited to ability to re-establish due to familiarity and no evidence of impediments.
propositions.quote: Contrary to Mr. Shah’s submission that the Officer assumed that he had a social network in India, the Officer made no such findings or assumptions... no evidence of any impediments to do so.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the Officer conducted a global assessment without contradictory findings and made no assumptions about social networks in India.

propositions.text: Officer noted Mr. Shah’s age throughout decision, including background, assessment, and conclusion, informing H&C factor assessment.
propositions.quote: the Officer noted Mr. Shah’s age at the outset of the decision... later in the assessment... and again in the conclusion... The Officer’s assessment... was informed by Mr. Shah’s personal circumstances, including his age.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah’s circumstances differ from Makarenko where failure to consider age made conclusions unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Contrary to Mr. Shah’s submissions, his circumstances differ from those in Makarenko where Justice Manson found that the Officer’s failure to consider the applicant’s age... made the other conclusions unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the Officer considered Mr. Shah’s age throughout, unlike in Makarenko where age was ignored making conclusions unreasonable.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah’s reliance on Epstein is misplaced; in Epstein, clear evidence of dependency existed unlike here where evidence was scant.
propositions.quote: With respect to Mr. Shah’s reliance on Epstein... no two cases are identical... In Epstein... there was clear evidence of the applicant’s dependency... In the present case... little evidence to support the claims...

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Mr. Shah’s reliance on Epstein misplaced due to lack of clear dependency evidence here.

propositions.text: Officer acknowledged some hardship from family separation but some hardship is inevitable and insufficient alone for H&C relief.
propositions.quote: The Officer acknowledged that Mr. Shah would experience some hardship arising from the separation from his family, but as noted in Kanthasamy at para 23, some hardship is inevitable and does not, on its own, warrant H&C relief.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the Officer acknowledged inevitable hardship from family separation, which alone does not warrant H&C relief.

propositions.text: Kanthasamy requires assessing the BIOC well identified and examined in light of all evidence in H&C applications
propositions.quote: In Kanthasamy, the Supreme Court of Canada (citing Baker at paras 74-75) reiterated the importance of assessing the BIOC in the context of an H&C application and noted that it is not enough to simply state that the interests have been considered. The child’s best interests must be well identified and examined in light of all the evidence (Kanthasamy, at para 39).

paragraphs.summary: Kanthasamy requires assessing the BIOC well identified and examined in light of all evidence in H&C applications, says prior court authority.

propositions.text: Officer was alert, alive and sensitive to younger grandson’s best interests and assessed BIOC in light of evidence
propositions.quote: I do not agree with Mr. Shah’s submission that the Officer was not “alert, alive and sensitive” to his younger grandson’s best interests. Clearly the Officer assessed the BIOC in light of the evidence presented.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer was alert and sensitive to the younger grandson’s best interests and assessed BIOC properly.

propositions.text: Officer set out appropriate approach to BIOC analysis in H&C: establish best interests, determine compromise, weigh BIOC in overall application
propositions.quote: The Officer set out an appropriate approach to a BIOC analysis in the context of an H&C application; first, to establish what is in the child’s best interests; second, to determine the degree to which those interests would be compromised by one decision over the other; and, finally, to determine the weight that should be attached to the BIOC in the overall H&C application.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer set out an appropriate approach to BIOC analysis in H&C applications.

propositions.text: Officer followed approach, found younger grandson’s best interests are to be with parents and have basic needs met, noting little evidence
propositions.quote: The Officer followed that approach, determining that the best interests of the younger grandson are to be around his parents and to have his basic needs met, including education, medical care, and social support from family and friends. The Officer addressed the evidence that was before him, noting that there was little.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer followed the approach and determined the younger grandson’s best interests properly.

propositions.text: Officer considered evidence of close relationship between Mr. Shah and grandson, including photographs over years
propositions.quote: Contrary to Mr. Shah’s submission, the Officer considered the evidence submitted to support the close relationship between Mr. Shah and his grandson, including the photographs of the two together over the years.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer considered evidence of Mr. Shah’s close relationship with his grandson, including photos.

propositions.text: Officer acknowledged Mr. Shah lived with younger grandson most of his life and gave positive weight to family ties
propositions.quote: The Officer also clearly acknowledged that Mr. Shah had lived with his younger grandson for most of his grandson’s life. In addition, the Officer gave significant positive weight to family ties, which also acknowledged the relationship he had with his grandsons.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer acknowledged Mr. Shah’s cohabitation and gave positive weight to family ties.

propositions.text: Officer not required to infer younger grandson’s best interests negatively affected from older grandson’s letter which did not mention younger grandson
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah’s argument that the Officer should have relied on the letter from his older grandson, which described their particular relationship, to infer that the same relationship existed with his younger grandson and that his younger grandson’s interests would be negatively impacted, ignores the principle that the onus is on Mr. Shah to establish that H&C considerations justify the exemption from the requirements of the Act. The Officer was not required to read between the lines or draw an inference that the younger grandson’s best interests would be negatively affected. The letter from the older grandson did not even mention the younger grandson.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer was not required to infer younger grandson’s interests were negatively affected from older grandson’s letter.

propositions.text: Officer considered relevant factors including grandson’s age and role of Mr. Shah in grandson’s life; no merit to argument ignoring these
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah’s argument that the Officer focussed on irrelevant factors, such as the availability of medical care and education for his grandson, yet ignored relevant factors such as his grandson’s age and the role played by Mr. Shah in his grandson’s life and cultural education is without merit. The Officer considered the factors set out in the Guidelines to the extent that they applied. The Officer clearly noted the grandson’s age. The Officer noted that – other than the photographs and the letters which described that they had all previously lived together ‒ there was little evidence that the younger grandson’s needs would not be met by his family in Canada, even in Mr. Shah’s absence.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer considered relevant factors including grandson’s age and Mr. Shah’s role; argument ignoring these is without merit.

propositions.text: Officer’s decision is justified, transparent and intelligible; exemption from Act not warranted; other options noted; judicial review dismissed
propositions.quote: In conclusion, the Officer’s decision is justified, transparent and intelligible. While sympathetic to the plight of Mr. Shah and his desire to remain with his family in Canada, the Officer reasonably found that an exemption from the requirements of the Act was not warranted. The Officer noted other options that Mr. Shah could pursue, including another online interest to sponsor or an application for the Parent and Grandparent Super Visa. JUDGMENT in file IMM-6078-18 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: The Application for Judicial Review is dismissed. There is no question proposed for certification.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Officer’s decision is justified and dismisses the judicial review application.
